title: What was on Mikasa’s menu—and why 156 people fell ill
dek: Rice and barley, salmon, and beef with potatoes were on Mikasa’s menu on 30 May 1904. The canned salmon had spoiled.

sections.title: Lunch at a forward base
paragraphs: Rice and barley, miso soup with dried daikon and tea for breakfast. More rice for lunch, this time with stewed canned salmon and hijiki seaweed, pickles and barley tea. For dinner, hardtack and roast beef with potatoes. That was Mikasa’s menu on 30 May 1904.

The ship was then at a forward base among the islands south of Liaodong. After taking part in the blockade of Port Arthur, she had been undergoing maintenance there since 10 May. Japanese historian Akinori Ishihara described the episode in his 2024 study of naval supply.

sections.title: Even canned food can spoil
paragraphs: After that lunch, 156 people aboard fell ill. Ishihara attributes the food poisoning to the canned salmon: its storage life had been exceeded and the contents had spoiled. Canned food was useful because it could be kept in reserve for a long time. But even those reserves had their limits.

Nor was this an isolated case. Food poisoning occurred aboard other Japanese ships in May and June 1904. Spoiled canned food and mouldy bread were among the causes; sometimes the offending food could not be identified. Aboard Mikasa, efforts were made to serve cooked food.

sections.title: Two supply ships were not enough
paragraphs: Two ships, Matsuyama Maru and Fukuoka Maru, were to supply the fleet. The plan was to deliver provisions to the forward forces roughly every six days. In practice, the warships operated in dispersed groups, and two supply ships proved too few.

Kotohira Maru and other vessels were brought in during August 1904. But adding a ship did not automatically make it a fully equipped food transport. Storing provisions required equipment, and the lack of it limited how much food could be carried. Getting the cargo to the right warship was only part of the job. It also had to arrive fit to eat.

limitations: The menu and number of people taken ill come from Ishihara’s 2024 study. The archival medical volume he cites has not been checked separately; 156 is the number of food-poisoning cases, not deaths.
The source does not establish exactly how this batch of canned salmon was stored. Linking its spoilage to the shortage of supply ships would require further investigation.

sources.title: Ship Logistics During the Russo-Japanese War: Rice Balls Were Served for a Post-Victory Dinner
sources.author: Akinori Ishihara (石原明徳), National Institute for Defense Studies, Japan
sources.locator: NIDS Commentary, No. 324. Pages 7–8; note 13 on page 10. Printed page numbers match the PDF page numbers.
sources.note: Original title: 日露戦争における艦のロジスティクス―勝ち戦の夕食は握飯. A modern study based on naval documents. The menu, food-poisoning episode and supply ships are described with attribution to the author; the original medical volume has not been checked separately.

title: Money in Dairen: who could get a loan?
dek: Silver bearing portraits of Yuan Shikai and Sun Yat-sen, Japanese banknotes and private credit firms. Bank clerk Sun Yaoting recalled a city with many kinds of money, where getting a loan was far from easy.

sections.title: Before converting the sum
paragraphs: How much would that be in today’s money? In our note on the tsarist ruble, the answers varied with the method of calculation. But before converting a sum, we need to know what people paid with. In Dairen under Japanese rule, several kinds of money were in use at once.

Sun Yaoting tells us about them. He had lived in Dalian since childhood and worked in banking from 1930. Starting as an apprentice and clerk, he eventually rose to senior positions. He knew the city’s banking life from the inside.

He names his workplace as Longkou, a joint Japanese-Chinese bank. He left an address too: Tianjin Street, as it was called when his account was recorded. Mergers and new bank names followed. Sun later described all this in the second issue of Materials on the History of Dalian. He also recalled which money the townspeople used—and who could borrow it.

sections.title: Silver portraits and paper gold
paragraphs: His list includes silver coins bearing portraits of Yuan Shikai and Sun Yat-sen, small silver coins, copper money and banknotes. He calls the Japanese paper money jinpiao, 金票. There is gold in the name, but these were notes, not gold coins.

Japanese banknotes predominated, Sun says. Chinese banks also issued paper money, but local issues required permission from the Japanese authorities and could serve only as temporary means of payment.

sections.title: Money in the city, money for its people
paragraphs: Sun describes Dairen as a city of manufacturing and trade with a constant need for money. Those seeking loans turned to the banks. But for an ordinary Chinese resident, he recalled, getting a bank loan was difficult: without enough collateral, there was little chance.

Loans were also available from qianzhuang, 钱庄, traditional private credit firms. They too required collateral and, Sun says, charged more interest than the banks. He writes separately about private moneylenders operating outside both banks and qianzhuang. Here his account grows particularly sharp: an expensive loan could bring ruin in a short time.

limitations: Pages 49–53 of the library PDF were used, not the whole article. The publication date of the collection’s second issue has not been established. Tianjin Street is the name given by the memoirist; the exact building has not been identified.

This is a bank clerk’s later account, with pronounced anticolonial and class-based judgements, rather than a picture of all Chinese residents’ experience. Exact interest rates are not given here: their basis of calculation has not been checked. Currency circulation under Japanese rule cannot be applied to Russian Dalny or to Russian prices in 1913.

sources.title: Finance in Colonial Dalian under Japanese Rule. Materials on the History of Dalian, Issue 2
sources.author: Sun Yaoting (孙耀庭)
sources.date: Publication date of the issue not established
